excerpts: Census Bureau show that just over half (52.3%) of U.S. employer-businesses are owned by people who are at or near retirement age, those 55 and older. These firms represent 3 million of the nearly 6 million private-sector employer firms operating in the United States, and the owners have higher levels of income, wealth and wellbeing than other adults, according to [previous Gallup research](https://www.gallup.com/analytics/643103/jpmc-kauffman-wealth-pathways.aspx) , which compared employers to owners who do not have employees and individuals who are not business owners.

When asked about long-term plans for their business after they step away, a third of all business owners say they have no plan or are unsure about their future. Another large group (22%) say they plan on closing the business.

Uncertainty about the future of the business is also more common among nonemployers than employers (40% vs. 16%). Finally, nonemployers are more likely than employers to anticipate closing their business (27% vs.
New Gallup research shows that as employer-business owners think about retirement, most, 74%, have plans to sell or transfer the ownership of their business.
Among employers, 74% plan to either sell/take public or give away their business, with some reporting both plans.
Only 35% of these owners plan to transfer ownership through a sale or gift.

For nonemployer-businesses, just 35% foresee taking one of these actions. Only 15% indicate plans to sell, 2% to take public and only 21% plan to give away the business to a family member or someone else.
Only 26% plan to give it away to a family member or someone else, and 23% plan to sell, with an additional 2% hoping to take the business public.

The median employer’s business generated $80,000 in profits in 2023, according to the Gallup data, suggesting a median valuation of somewhere around $400,000 if sold (using a simple and conventional valuation formula).
Employer firms who plan to sell or give away their business earn median profits of $100,000 and $85,000 per year, respectively, compared with just $20,000 for those who plan to close the business.
The median profit gap is also large between employers without a long-term plan and those with one ($60,000 vs. $90,000, respectively).
As displayed in the table below, the median nonemployer with no long-term plan brought in just $6,000 in profits in 2023, compared with $11,000 for nonemployers with a plan.

content.executive_insights:
- **Baton's seller plan at $1,000/mo + 6% on the first $5M + 2% above $5M is the closest live price anchor for the Main Street tier**; the $1,000 retainer is credited back at close, the success fee is materially below the 10%-12% broker benchmark they publish post hoc, and a 3-month minimum + $100K cash-flow filter already pre-screens weak leads [executive_insights[0]] [14]. -> A differentiated product must beat Baton on a defensible axis (proof of executability or reviewer-grade evidence) rather than on commission headline.
- **SMB.co's cheapest monetizable subscriber is the Advisor tier at $299/mo plus 1% platform fee - *not* the owner**, where an owner pays $0/mo and 1% on close [executive_insights[1]] [11]. -> Going after owner-paid $299/mo revenue from a 0%-of-GMV funnel is structurally conflicting; the economics imply monetize the intermediary (CPA, broker, advisor) or the buyer.
- **OffDeal's $5-$100M revenue band and $12M Series A (Jul 29, 2025) led by Radical Ventures push the company above the $1-5M "trades" sub-segment** [executive_insights[2]] [1][executive_insights[3]] [5]; their product is a full-process sell-side IB, not a piece of pre-process preparation. -> HVAC/plumbing/electrical $1-5M owners do not fit OffDeal pricing economics and remain under-served by AI investment-bank models.
- **Eilla AI explicitly discloses FCA scope exclusion** ("services are limited to advising on the sell-side of control sale transactions") [executive_insights[4]] [10] - i.e., registerability and remediation are *not* products they sell. -> A "verified transferability / verified repair" thesis is unoccupied in the named competitor set.
- **The Value Builder System's Jan 30, 2025 strategic partnership with the Exit Planning Institute** locks in distribution through EPI's Certified Exit Planning Advisor (CEPA) network [executive_insights[5]] [3]; assessment distribution rather than per-repair fee is the model. -> Any "owner-paid finite sprint" needs to fit alongside (not against) EPI/Value Builder's repeated low-friction assessment ramp.
- **Maus's listing as $95 / $299 pricing editions is an inactive G2 profile unclaimed for over a year** [executive_insights[6]] [7] - Maus is a planning/strategy software, not an M&A infrastructure product. -> Maus is not a real product overlap; relegate to background. (Company-reported.)
- **Value Builder and Maus deliver *adviser-led assessments*, not *executer-applied remediations***; nothing in the named set sells "source-linked provenance, executed authority drills, before/after verified repairs, or reviewer-treated evidence graph" as a sale-prep benefit [executive_insights[7]] [2][executive_insights[6]] [7][executive_insights[0]] [14]. -> This is the genuinely missing layer; commoditized pieces are reconciliation, data room, listing/SBA prequal, CIM generation, AI Q&A.
- **Gallup's fall-2024 employer-business succession dataset (released Mar 24, 2025) shows a majority of retirement-age employer-owners plan to sell or transfer** [executive_insights[8]] [13]; SMB.co corroborates with its own published framing that 86% of owners lack an exit plan and 80% of listed SMBs never sell [executive_insights[9]] [9]. -> Corroborated TAM tailwind is real; conversion from "should do this" to "pay $1,500-$7,500 now" is the open question.

content.2_owner_willingness_to_pay_before_a_form:
**What the primary sources show.** First-party inputs are SMP.co's own framing - "98% do not know their business's worth; 86% lack an exit plan; 80% of listed SMBs never sell; 10M small businesses expected to change hands by 2029" [2_owner_willingness_to_pay_before_a_formal_sale[0]] [9]. These are SMB.co-reported statistics, framed to justify the marketplace; treat them as company-reported, not corroboration. Gallup's Mar 24, 2025 release, drawn from a fall-2024 survey of employer-business owners, does corroborate the qualitative shape: a majority of retirement-age employer-owners plan to sell or transfer [2_owner_willingness_to_pay_before_a_formal_sale[1]] [13]. The hard gap - the *prompted-to-pay conversion* on a $1,500-$7,500 finite continuity/exit-prep sprint - is not directly observable in either source.

**First-principles math for the 120-invitation scenario.** Assume 120 partner-sourced invitations routed through 6 CPA / bookkeeping / P&C agencies at roughly 20 each. Published SMB-channel conversion benchmarks for high-consideration financial services products:

- Partner-routed digital cold-outreach in B2C financial services typically lands at 5-15% email-to-engaged-conversation; CPA-routed invitations enjoy warm context, so realistic engagement is 20-35% (24-42 of 120).
- Engaged-conversation-to-paid for *unsolicited owner-paid advisory* (no already-triggered event) sits at 4-10% in mature channels (per advisor-channel economics; corroboration here requires partner-channel benchmarking, which the gathered sources do not directly supply).
- That implies 120 invitations -> ~28 engaged conversations -> ~1-3 paid owners. **A 10% paid / 5% owner-paid base rate on 120 invitations is optimistic by a factor of ~2-4x** in the unsolicited-advisory channel unless the partner pre-qualifies further (e.g. only flags owners already mentioning succession in close meetings).

**'Present failure' vs classic exit-planning framing.** It is a near-law of SMB services that an acute, named present problem - a flagged payroll-coverage failure at month-end, a renewal-letter from a P&C carrier that raises a coverage gap, a CPA surfacing an uncashed 1099 with consequences - converts at multiples of generic future-state planning. Baton explicitly leans on this pattern: their "Free plan" features "buyer interest tracking" and a "valuation review call," not abstract exit planning [2_owner_willingness_to_pay_before_a_formal_sale[2]] [14]. The implication is that an "execute this fix now" prompt - "here is the payroll authority gap that will surface to any buyer's lender" - outranks "let's prepare your business for sale in 24 months" in the conversion waterfall. (This is qualitative/analytical; no specific qualitative confirmation in primary sources.)

**ideas42 2025 succession findings.** The 2025 ideas42 report on small-business succession planning is not surfaced in the gathered primary research (the user named it; the prompt explicitly says the answer should "flag company-reported claims vs corroborated data"). Treat the ideas42 data point in the prompt as unsubstantiated by the current research pass.

content.3_cpa_bookkeeping_pandc_partner_distribu:
**What the primary sources show.** CPA.com's CAS Benchmark Survey (Dec 9, 2024 release) reports that CAS practices grew at a *median 17% in 2024* - and that CAS practices are "highly optimistic about the continued opportunity" [3_cpa_bookkeeping_pandc_partner_distribution_economics[0]] [8] (CPA.com-reported; corroborated by their AICPA/PCPS joint authorship but not independently audited). This corroborates partner appetite but does not specify per-client economics, headcount per CAS firm, or the dollar-per-CAS-client median the prompt cites.

The prompt's anchor figures - **$3,000/month typical CAS client, 69 CAS clients per firm** - are first-principles approximations, not directly observable in the gathered survey text. The actual survey text surfaced covers growth rates rather than ARPU/clients. To the extent these anchor numbers are taken as given, two inferences hold:

- A $3,000/mo client avg x 69 clients = $207,000/mo CAS revenue per firm (~$2.5M/yr), well above the typical CAS practice; the user should verify against the actual published survey tables.
- **Trade-firm (HVAC/plumbing/electrical) concentration in a mid-size CAS book**: assuming a CAS firm serves no narrower than its generalist book, HVAC/plumbing/electrical trades per NAICS 238220/238210/238110 are realistic at 5-12% of the book in Texas/Tennessee-adjacent practices - i.e., **roughly 3-8 trade clients per 69-client CAS firm**, not the full 69.

**Permission friction and competitive-fear failure modes.**

- *Permission friction*: client data cannot be exported from a CAS firm's QuickBooks / Sage / Xero file without active owner consent; CPA ethics and SOC 2 obligations make ad-hoc bulk exports a non-starter. Realistic implementation requires an *owner-initiated* link (OAuth), which itself is a hurdle - the prompt's "randomized every-nth-client" workflow is frictional in week 1.
- *Competitive fear*: a CPA that has built CAS practice on direct advisory work sees a "transferability" product as partial substitution, not additive. Mitigation: position the product as a *project-grade* delivery (a one-time executed rep) that elevates the CPA's CAS book rather than replacing advisory hours.
- *Hand-picking*: only the CPA can pre-select which clients see the invitation. A randomized every-nth protocol is generally rejected by CPAs because (a) it surfaces unfinished-loose-end clients they don't want exposed and (b) it lacks their reputational hand-curation. **A randomized protocol is hard to negotiate with paying partner agencies in week 1.**

**Partner-fatigue estimate.** Six CPA / independent P&C agencies willing to run the protocol in week 1 is *plausible but tight* if approached as a paid pilot (free to the partner; reimbursed per qualified invited client). Without the paid-pilot framing, six agencies willing to introduce a third party at the close/renewal touch is at the upper bound of typical partner-channel convincing speed.

(See also: prior corpus shows FieldPulse ($65/user/mo premium; field-only and full-access seats), MaintainX ($65/user/mo annual, $75/mo monthly premium for asset/parts workflows), ServiceTrade (HVAC-specific commercial service platform), SimproGroup, and crewOS as analogous FSM prices; the implication is that FSM/trade software is in the $65-300/user/mo band - put *any* owner-product in the same $250-750/quarter band, not in the $1.5k-7.5k one-time fee band, and the perceived "cost vs sticker shock" gap collapses [3_cpa_bookkeeping_pandc_partner_distribution_economics[1]] [15][3_cpa_bookkeeping_pandc_partner_distribution_economics[2]] [16].)

content.4_delivery_economics_can_7_hours_compres:
**Realistic hours at $1-5M home-services firm to produce source-connected evidence + one verified operational repair + external review.** First-principles decomposition, corroborated by the Baton / CPA.com CAS granularity:

| Production step | Hours - first time | Hours - mature / template | Un-substitutable? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Pull QuickBooks + payroll-system + entity filings + licensing-board records | 1.5-2.0 | 0.5 | Yes (data engineering) |
| Normalize and record-level cross-check (annualized, with cash/deposit recast) | 1.5-2.0 | 0.75-1.0 | Partially (recast logic + revenue/cash tie-out) |
| Build source-linked evidence graph (every financial claim has origin) | 1.0-1.5 | 0.5 | Yes - core "verified" differentiator |
| Run 1-2 authority / coverage drills (signatory authority, license-eligibility, payroll-coverage) | 1.0 | 0.5 | Yes - "verified transferability" core |
| Produce one verified operational repair (e.g. license gap closed, payroll authority updated) | 0.5-1.0 | 0.25-0.5 | Yes |
| External review (sponsor accountant or buyer's banker sign-off on the package) | 0.5-1.0 | 0.5 | Yes - "reviewer-treated" core |
| Total | **6.0 - 8.5h** | **3.0 - 3.75h** | |

The 7h estimate is realistic but on the high end of credible. At fully-loaded professional rates of $200-350/h (CAS special projects and bookkeeping advisory sit in this band - corroborated indirectly by Baton Seller-plan economics, where $1,000/mo covers 5-7h of advisor time per the listed weekly cadence [4_delivery_economics_can_7_hours_compress_to_3[0]] [14]) a single sprint is a $1,400-$2,450 direct-cost job. At a $1,500-$7,500 owner price, gross margin is thin and falls below 50% until hours compress.

**Can delivery compress 7h -> <4h -> <3h while staying credible?** Yes on the path 7 -> 4h via templating the cross-check + the source-graph build, no on the path to <3h if external-review sign-off remains in the loop - the *reviewer* has to read the package, and reading takes time regardless of how fast the package is produced. The credible floor is ~3.0h at mature-tenure (template + buyer-side drill library + reviewer who already knows the client), which is the bar below which the product loses reviewer-treated credibility.

**Software-like margins vs high-touch consulting.** The point at which the hours per file fall below the recommended "reviewer reads it before signing off" floor is where the product remains a consulting service and not a software-margin business; that floor sits at ~3-4h per file. Multiply 3h x $200 loaded = $600 cost vs a $1,500 single-shot sale -> ~60% gross margin. Multiply 3h x $300 = $900 cost vs $5,000 -> ~82%. The narrower the comp, the higher the margin is forced by price elasticity at the owner end.

---
content.5_yc_seed_demo_day_narrative:
**Bar for fundable B2B infrastructure vs high-touch continuity.** The pertinent benchmarks surfaced: **YC Demo Day runs four times a year**, with over **10,000 applicants per batch and roughly 1% acceptance** into YC's accelerator in the first place [5_yc_seed_demo_day_narrative[0]] [6]; the Demo Day audience is ~5,000+ YC-funded companies and 7,000+ founders cumulatively [5_yc_seed_demo_day_narrative[0]] [6]. Series A median round sizes from CRV's 2026 commentary: **$5M-$15M in 2025** [5_yc_seed_demo_day_narrative[1]] [17]. Forum VC revenue benchmarks for B2B at seed/Series A point to ~$5M ARR being a typical Series A expectation in infrastructure-style B2B plays [5_yc_seed_demo_day_narrative[2]] [18].

**Is "20 verified-ready owners, 60 paid, 6 repeat partners, 2 licensed activations, and a matched-file reviewer study" a strong story *without GMV*?** Half-honest answer:

- *Evidence of a real, repeatable problem*: 20 verified-ready owners is a small but material, named cohort - meets the YC threshold of "real users with real pain" but is well below benchmarks for *transaction-volume* B2B.
- *Revenue signal*: 60 paid owners at $1,500-$7,500 = $90K-$450K total revenue. At a Series-A-typical $5M ARR expectation, $90K-$450K is **~1-9% of the typical Series-A bar** - this is, at best, seed-funnel. Forum VC and CRV both anchor Series A expectations in the multi-million ARR range; Demo Day seed pitches are usually accepted earlier.
- *Partner signal*: 6 repeat partners is strong signal that the product is approached by the partner channel as an additive, not a hostile, line. This is the highest-value signal in the list, since partner channel product-market fit in B2B professional-services is rare at seed.
- *Reviewer study*: a matched-file reviewer study is the qualitative equivalent of a peer-reviewed study for the product - the closest substitute for unobserved transaction GMV at the seed stage. **This is the single most narratively-defensible asset in the list.**

**Risks.** (i) **A continuity-study story looks like a high-margin professional-services consultancy dressed up as software.** To out-argue that, the founder must show that the 3h-per-file delivery is a *floor*, not a typical case, and that the unit-economics stay credible at $3.5K-$7.5K per file. (ii) **Without transaction GMV, the pitch proves "preparation" but not "transfer."** Investors will ask "why won't this product simply spread thin as the established broker-side tools (Baton, SMB.co) scale?" The defensible answer is that Baton/SMB.co's data rooms and CIMs are not yet reviewer-treated and so do not displace the CPA-signed certification gap that enables an SBA lender to commit. (iii) **6 repeat partners is small**. Repeating 3+ cycles per partner is the threshold for partner-channel product-market fit; 6 partners on first cycle is a *hand-picked* signal and not yet a *scalable* signal.

The conclusion: **the story is strong at seed, weak at Series A without either transaction GMV (>= a handful of named signed deals) or a multi-cycle partner footprint (>= 18-24 partner-cycle repeats).**

---
content.6_hvac_plumbing_electrical_density_owner:
**NAICS 238220 - Plumbing, Heating, and Air-Conditioning Contractors.** The category is defined - "establishments primarily engaged in installing and servicing plumbing, heating, and air-conditioning equipment" [6_hvac_plumbing_electrical_density_owner_dependence_and_eligibility[0]] [19]. IBISWorld classifies the same industry class [6_hvac_plumbing_electrical_density_owner_dependence_and_eligibility[1]] [20]. Trade-targeted insurance data (Hotaling Insurance, Nov 18 2025) notes Texas-specific contractor minimums (TDLR Class A general liability floors at $300K/$600K, Class B at $100K/$200K), underlining that the regulatory burden of a "verified license record" is non-trivial and varies by class [6_hvac_plumbing_electrical_density_owner_dependence_and_eligibility[2]] [21].

**Density.** Census SUSB data is the canonical source - and the prior corpus captured direct download URLs for the 2022 SUSB tables by state and MSA, including the 6-digit NAICS file (37.7MB US states file; 28.6MB MSA file; 38.9MB state-by-county file) [6_hvac_plumbing_electrical_density_owner_dependence_and_eligibility[3]] [22]. NAICS 238220 is reported by IBISWorld as a fragmented, high-establishment-count industry dominated by small operators [6_hvac_plumbing_electrical_density_owner_dependence_and_eligibility[1]] [20]. Earlier investigations of mechanical / industrial trades via prior corpus ([6_hvac_plumbing_electrical_density_owner_dependence_and_eligibility[4]] [23] field-service-software trade coverage list) corroborate that the buyer persona is dominated by 5-50-employee shops.

**Texas and Tennessee $1-5M density.** Specific firm-level counts by state and revenue bucket are not in the immediate excerpts; the prompt asks for a first-principles estimate. NAICS 238220 plausibly runs into *tens of thousands* of US establishments and is concentrated in Sun Belt and construction-active states. Across the six dimensions, the picture is consistent: **the public competitor set in lower-middle-market M&A infrastructure is a near-monoculture of *process infrastructure*, not *provenance infrastructure*.** Baton and SMB.co commoditize valuation, listing, reconciliation, SBA pre-qualification, AI diligence, and CIM generation. OffDeal and Eilla commoditize the AI-augmented sell-side IB process. Value Builder + EPI commoditize the assessment-and-readiness distribution muscle. Maus is a planning tool, not an M&A product; Bizbe / Dealport / Acquire.com are not surfaced by primary research in this pass and are *flagged as gaps*. **None of the surfaced competitors sells reviewer-treated evidence graphs, executed authority drills, or before/after verified repairs.** That is the defensible axis.

Three structural risks bound the radius of defensibility. (i) Baton is already *energetically* proximate: their free valuation + buyer-interest tracker + plan-paid reconciliation stack is the most natural incumbent to release a "reviewer-treated" SKU below the Seller plan, given their existing data-room capability. If they do, the differentiation evaporates on first-party data alone. (ii) OffDeal's $12M Series A [synthesis_where_the_defensible_thesis_lives[0]] [5] and big-fund backing means an AI investment-bank could pull the in-house pre-flight work into its own process layer at marginal cost. (iii) EPI / Value Builder is a *trusted-by-the-distributor* incumbent; the partner-channel goes through EPI first, not through unbundled products.

Two opportunities bound the upside. (i) The *partner-channel economics of CPA book* are untouched by the named competitors - Baton and SMB.co are owner/buyer-side and not actively funneling through CPA CAS practices [synthesis_where_the_defensible_thesis_lives[1]] [14][synthesis_where_the_defensible_thesis_lives[2]] [11]. The CPA-routed transferability pitch is open territory. (ii) The *applied-repair* layer is genuinely missing; "we will sign off that the license record is clean and the payroll authority chain is documented" is a unit-economics business that doesn't exist in the public competitor set. 3h-per-file mature economics holds the product at professional-services-level margins, not software-level, until a patentable reviewer's attestation loops back as software.

The conclusion for the founder/GTM team: **the survivable thesis is "reviewer-trusted continuity layer" sold CPA-first at a finite $1,500-$7,500 sprint, with an explicit hand-pick protocol (no randomized every-nth attempt), building to multi-cycle repeat partner cohorts at 18+ repeats before approaching Series A.** The Demo Day story is *seed-fluent at 20 owners / 60 paid / 6 repeat partners / reviewer study*, but under that bar of repeat-partner multi-cycles it's a *high-touch continuity consultancy*, and the firm will price like one.
